t: The after-loss checklist: what to do, in order
pre: Most of it can wait. Here's what can't.

b.p: In the days after a loss, the to-do list can feel endless. It helps to know that most of it can wait weeks, and only a handful of things need doing right away.

timeline: If they died at home under hospice, call the hospice nurse. If it was unexpected, call 911. Tell close family, choose a funeral home, and secure the home, car and any pets.
Order death certificates (the funeral home usually does this). Find the will. Tell their employer. Hold off on any big decisions.
Notify Social Security, banks, insurers and the credit bureaus. Claim any life insurance. Cancel subscriptions.
Start probate if needed, close or transfer accounts, retitle the house and car, and file a final tax return by the next April 15.

b.tip: You don't have to do this alone, or all at once. Pick one person to keep a simple list of who's been told.

t: Where do people actually store their passwords?
pre: The honest answer, with pros and cons.

b.p: There's no single right answer. What matters is that one trusted person could get in if they had to.

table: Lots of accounts, strong passwords, emergency access features
Someone still needs the one master password
People who prefer paper; easy for family to use
Keep it locked away, and update it when passwords change
Tied to one device and one login
Easy to find, easy to lose, rarely encrypted

b.p: Many people use a mix: a password manager for everyday logins, plus a sealed note in the binder with the master password and phone passcode.

t: Payable-on-death (POD): what it means
pre: One free form that can skip months of court.

b.p: A payable-on-death (POD) designation lets you name who gets the money in a bank account when you die. It's usually free, takes a few minutes, and the money passes to them directly, without going through probate.

steps: You add a POD beneficiary to your checking, savings or CD account.
Nothing changes while you're alive. It's still your money, and the beneficiary can't touch it.
After you die, they bring a death certificate and ID to the bank.
The bank pays them directly. No court, no waiting for the estate.

b.tip: A POD beneficiary overrides your will for that account. If your will says one thing and the POD form says another, the form usually wins.
POD is for cash accounts. The same idea for investments, and in many states a home or car, is called transfer-on-death (TOD). Rules vary by state, so it's worth checking what yours allows.

t: Closing accounts after a death: the order that saves time
pre: Do these in this order and you'll make fewer calls.

b.p: Closing someone's accounts is slow, but a sensible order saves a lot of repeated calls.

steps: Gather paperwork first. Several certified death certificates (official copies with a raised or printed seal, usually ordered through the funeral home), plus letters testamentary (the court document that proves you're the executor), if there's probate.
Stop anything that costs money or could be misused. Credit cards, subscriptions, and auto-payments.
Contact the banks. Joint and POD accounts pass directly. Others may be frozen until the executor is confirmed.
Utilities and home services. Transfer or cancel, depending on what happens to the house.
Phone and email last. Security codes often go to that phone number and inbox, so keep them until everything else is done.

b.tip: Keep a log with the company, date, who you spoke to, and a reference number. It stops you having to repeat the same call three times.

t: Your phone passcode: the six digits that hold everything
pre: Phone makers can't unlock it for your family.

b.p: A phone holds contacts, photos, banking apps, and the security codes that unlock nearly every other account. Without the passcode, much of that can be out of reach.
Apple and Google generally won't unlock a device for family, even with a death certificate. At most, they can help reset it, which wipes what's on it.

list: Your phone passcode
Your phone carrier account PIN (needed to move the number and receive security codes)
Where your backup codes or password manager details are kept

b.tip: Keep these on paper in a sealed envelope in your binder, not in a notes app on the same phone.

t: How to bring it up without making it weird
pre: One sentence is enough to start.

b.p: Most people put off telling family about their plan because they don't want it to feel heavy. It doesn't have to be a big conversation.

list: “I've put together a folder of where everything is, just in case. It's in the study. Nothing's wrong, I just didn't want you to have to guess.”
“I did my will and a few other things. Can I show you where it all is? Five minutes.”
“A friend's family had a hard time after their dad died, so I got organized. Here's what I did.”

b.p: People are usually relieved, not upset. Questions can come later.

t: New baby: guardians and beneficiaries
pre: The few updates that matter most.

b.p: A new baby changes what your plan needs to cover. These are the updates that matter most.

list: Name a guardian. This is normally done in a will. Ask the person first.
Consider life insurance. Term life is often the simplest, most affordable option for young families.
Check beneficiaries. Naming a young child directly can mean a court has to appoint someone to manage the money. A trust or a custodian (UTMA) avoids that.
Add their documents. Birth certificate and Social Security card locations go in your records.

b.tip: Laws vary by state. An estate attorney can set up a guardian and trust together, often in a single meeting.

t: The subscriptions that kept charging
pre: Where the forgotten ones hide.

b.p: It's common. Months after a death, small charges are still going out: a gym, a cloud storage plan, a streaming service, an app nobody knew about. Each needs its own call to stop.

list: The last 12 months of bank and credit card statements (to catch yearly renewals)
App Store or Google Play subscriptions on their phone
PayPal automatic payments
Their email inbox: search for “receipt”, “renewal” and “subscription”

b.tip: Cancelling the card isn't always enough. Some card networks automatically pass new card details to merchants, so cancel subscriptions directly too.

t: Set up your phone's emergency info
pre: First responders can see it, even when your phone is locked.

b.p: Your phone can show your medical details and emergency contacts on the lock screen, with no passcode needed. In an emergency, that's how responders learn your allergies, your medications, and who to call.

steps: Open the Health app and tap your photo.
Tap Medical ID, then Edit.
Turn on Show When Locked and add emergency contacts.
Open Settings, then Safety & emergency.
Add medical information and emergency contacts.
Turn on lock screen access (the exact wording varies by phone).

t: The first 24–72 hours
pre: A short list for the hardest days.

b.p: In the first days, only a few things truly need doing. Everything else can wait.

list: Get a legal pronouncement of death. Hospitals and hospice handle this. For an unexpected death at home, call 911.
Tell close family and friends. Ask one person to help spread the word.
Choose a funeral home. They'll transport the body and help order death certificates. Check first for a prepaid plan or written wishes.
Secure the home and car. Lock up, take valuables, and ask a neighbor to keep an eye out.
Care for pets and dependents.

b.tip: You don't need to call banks or cancel anything yet. That can happen next week.

t: Password book vs. password manager: honest pros and cons
pre: Both work. Here's how to choose.

b.p: Both work. The right one is the one you'll actually keep up to date.

table: Free (Bitwarden, Apple Passwords, Google Password Manager) or about $20–40 a year
They need the master password, or an emergency access feature
Only if you write down every change
Updates when you change a password

b.p: A good middle ground: use a password manager day to day, and keep its master password in a sealed envelope in your binder.

b.tip: Never put passwords in your will. After probate, a will usually becomes a public record.

t: Apple Legacy Contact, step by step
pre: Five minutes so your family can reach your photos.

b.p: Apple Legacy Contact lets you choose who can access your iCloud data, like photos, messages, notes and files, after you die. Without it, your family may not be able to get to them at all.

steps: On your iPhone, open Settings and tap your name.
Tap Sign-In & Security, then Legacy Contact.
Tap Add Legacy Contact and choose someone.
Share the access key. You can send it in Messages, or print a copy for your binder.

b.p: When the time comes, your legacy contact will need the access key and a copy of your death certificate.

b.tip: Legacy Contact doesn't include passwords saved in your Keychain, or movies, music and books you've bought. Your phone passcode still needs to be written down.

t: How to add a POD beneficiary to a bank account
pre: Ten minutes, usually free.

b.p: Adding a payable-on-death (POD) beneficiary usually takes about ten minutes and costs nothing.

steps: Log in to your bank's website or app and look for “beneficiaries”, often under account settings or your profile.
Can't find it? Call or visit a branch and ask for a POD beneficiary form.
Add each person's full legal name. Some banks also ask for a date of birth, address or Social Security number.
Naming more than one person? Choose how to split it, for example 50/50.
Save or sign, and ask for a confirmation.

b.p: POD usually works on checking, savings, CDs and money market accounts. Investment accounts have a similar option called transfer-on-death (TOD).

b.tip: Write down which accounts have a POD beneficiary, and who it is, so your family knows to ask.

t: Bitwarden's free plan, set up in 15 minutes
pre: A free password manager with no time limit.

b.p: Bitwarden is a password manager with a free plan that never expires. It stores unlimited passwords and syncs them across all your devices.

steps: Go to bitwarden.com and create a free account.
Choose a master password. It's the one password you'll need to remember, so make it long. Four or five random words work well.
Install the app on your phone and the browser extension on your computer.
Start with the accounts that matter most: email, bank and phone carrier. Add the rest as you log in to them.
Write your master password on paper and seal it in your binder.

b.tip: Emergency access, which lets a trusted person request your vault after a waiting period, is only on the paid Premium plan ($19.80 a year as of 2026). On the free plan, the sealed master password in your binder does the same job.

t: Google Inactive Account Manager, step by step
pre: Decide what happens to your Gmail, Photos and Drive.

b.p: Google's Inactive Account Manager decides what happens to your Google account, including Gmail, Photos and Drive, if you stop using it.

steps: Open any Google app, tap your profile picture, then Manage your Google Account.
Go to Data & privacy, then Make a plan for your digital legacy.
Choose how long Google waits before acting. The default is 3 months, and you can set it up to 18.
Add up to 10 people and choose what each one can download.
Choose whether your account is deleted afterward.

b.tip: Google will email and text you before it acts. Keep your recovery phone number and email up to date so a reminder doesn't go unseen.

t: Tell one person where the binder is
pre: A plan only helps if someone can find it.

b.p: A plan only helps if someone can find it. You don't need a family meeting. One trusted person is enough.

list: Where the binder is, and where the key is if it's locked
Roughly what's inside
Where any sealed envelope with passwords is
Who else knows

b.p: “If anything ever happens to me, everything you need is in the blue binder in the hall closet. The key's in my desk drawer.” That's the whole conversation.

b.tip: If you ever move the binder, tell them again.

t: Where to keep your binder
pre: Safe, but not so safe nobody can get to it.

b.p: Your binder needs to be safe, but not so safe that nobody can get to it.

table: Check the rating. Many protect paper for 30–60 minutes.
No protection from fire or water
Can be hard to open after a death unless someone else is on the box
They need to keep it private

b.p: Most people keep it at home in a fire-resistant safe or box, and tell one person where the key is.

b.tip: Don't keep your only copy of your will in a safe deposit box. Some banks won't open the box without it.

t: Life insurance beneficiaries, and why your will doesn't override them
pre: The form wins, not the will.

b.p: Life insurance pays whoever is named on the policy's beneficiary form, not whoever is named in your will. The insurer pays them directly, usually without probate.
That's why an old form matters. An ex-spouse, a parent who has died, or no one at all may still be listed.

list: Primary beneficiary: who gets it first
Contingent beneficiary: who gets it if the primary has died
Percentages, if you've named more than one person
Workplace policies, often set up on your first day and forgotten

b.tip: If no beneficiary is alive or named, the money usually goes to your estate and through probate. Naming a young child directly can mean a court has to appoint someone to manage it.

t: Ways to pass on assets without probate: one-page chart
pre: One form per account can skip the court.

b.p: Probate is the court process for settling an estate. It can take months and cost money. Many things you own can skip it with the right form.

table: Your bank, online or at a branch
Transfer-on-death deed (many states) or joint ownership with right of survivorship
Transfer-on-death title (some states) or joint ownership

b.tip: Rules vary by state, especially for homes and cars. A living trust is another way to keep many assets out of probate.

t: What a funeral really costs (and where the money goes)
pre: The median is several thousand dollars, and the price list is where the details live.

b.p: Funeral costs surprise many families, mostly because they arrive all at once and in the hardest week. Knowing what the pieces are makes the bill easier to read.

According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the national median cost of a funeral with a viewing and burial was $8,300 in 2023, and $6,280 for a funeral with cremation. Those figures don't include cemetery costs, such as the plot, opening the grave or a headstone, which are billed separately and can add thousands more.

table: The funeral home's staff, planning, permits and overhead. Every funeral home charges it, and it can't be declined.
Bringing the person from the place of death to the funeral home
Optional in most cases, but often required by the funeral home for a public viewing
Use of the facility and staff for a visitation or service
Transport to the service and cemetery
The plot, opening and closing the grave, a burial vault or liner, and a headstone, usually from the cemetery, not the funeral home

b.h: What families often look at to manage cost

list: Direct cremation or direct burial, which skip the viewing and are usually the lowest-cost options
Holding a memorial service later, at home or a place of worship
Buying a casket or urn from a third-party seller
Comparing price lists from two or three funeral homes

b.tip: Funeral homes must give you an itemized price list, under a federal rule. Asking for it before agreeing to anything lets families see the cost of each item and drop what they don't want.

Median funeral with cremation (2023, excl. cemetery)

t: Your rights with a funeral home: the FTC Funeral Rule
pre: A federal rule that lets families pick and choose.

b.p: The Funeral Rule is a federal regulation enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. It applies to funeral homes across the US and is meant to let families compare prices and pay only for what they want.

list: Prices by phone. A funeral home has to give price information over the phone if asked.
A written price list. Anyone who asks in person must get an itemized General Price List to keep.
Pick only what you want. Families can usually choose individual goods and services instead of a package, apart from the basic services fee.
Your own casket or urn. A funeral home can't refuse one bought elsewhere, or charge a fee for using it.
No false claims. A funeral home can't say embalming is required by law when it isn't. It's rarely required by law, though some funeral homes require it for a public viewing.
Cremation containers. Funeral homes offering direct cremation have to make an inexpensive alternative container available, rather than requiring a casket.

b.p: The rule applies to funeral homes. Cemeteries, crematories that don't sell funeral services, and third-party sellers generally aren't covered, though some states have their own rules for them.
Complaints can be filed with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and with the state board that licenses funeral directors.

b.tip: Bringing a friend who isn't grieving to the funeral home is common. They can ask about prices while the family focuses on the decisions.

t: Transportation and mileage charges: what to ask before you sign
pre: Getting from one place to another can add up quietly.

b.p: Several lines on a funeral bill are about moving the person or the family: from the place of death, to a service, to the cemetery or crematory. These charges are easy to miss until the final bill.

list: Transfer of remains: bringing the person from a home, hospital or care facility to the funeral home
Hearse: transport to the service and to the cemetery
Service car or van: carrying flowers, paperwork or equipment
Family limousine: optional cars for the family
Mileage: an extra charge per mile beyond a set distance
Out-of-state transport: shipping or driving the person to another state for burial
Is transfer of remains included in a package, or listed separately?
How many miles are included before mileage charges start, and what's the rate?
Is there an after-hours or weekend fee for the first transfer?
If the person died out of state, can a local funeral home there handle the transfer, and is that cheaper?
Are any of these optional?

b.p: Under the federal Funeral Rule, transfer of remains and the hearse each have to be listed with a price on the funeral home's General Price List, so the numbers can be compared before anything is signed.

b.tip: When someone dies far from home, families sometimes use two funeral homes: one near the place of death to handle the transfer, and one at home for the service. Asking both for prices can show which arrangement costs less.

t: Securing the home and car
pre: A quiet house and an unused car are both easy targets.

b.p: When someone lived alone, their home and car may sit empty for weeks after a death. Obituaries and funeral notices are public, and unfortunately some people watch them. A few simple steps can protect the house and what's in it.

list: Locking doors and windows, and collecting spare keys from neighbors, cleaners or caregivers
Changing locks if many people had keys
Throwing out perishable food and checking that the stove, heaters and water are off
Moving valuables, important papers and medications somewhere safe
Keeping lights on a timer and lawn or snow taken care of so the house looks lived in
Asking a neighbor to keep an eye on it during the funeral

b.p: Many homeowners policies limit coverage once a house has been empty for a while, often after 30 or 60 days. Calling the insurer to explain the situation is common, and they can say what the policy requires.

list: Keeping it in a garage or driveway, locked, with the keys somewhere safe
Keeping the insurance active until the car is sold or transferred
Not letting anyone drive it until the insurer confirms they're covered

b.tip: Executors usually aren't supposed to give away or sell belongings until they have legal authority. Securing things is fine; distributing them can wait.

t: Pausing and forwarding mail
pre: Mail is a map of every account. It also attracts identity thieves.

b.p: After a death, mail keeps arriving: bills, statements, renewals and junk. That mail is useful, because it shows which accounts exist. Left in an unattended mailbox, it can also be stolen and used for identity theft.

The US Postal Service lets the executor or estate administrator forward a deceased person's mail. This is usually done in person at the local post office, with proof of authority such as letters testamentary from the probate court. Rules and documents can vary, so checking with the local post office first is common.

b.h: Holding mail for a short time

b.p: For a short gap, such as the week of the funeral, a family member at the same address can request a USPS Hold Mail service online or at the post office.

The Association of National Advertisers runs a Deceased Do Not Contact list through DMAchoice.org. Registering a name there can reduce marketing mail over time, though it doesn't stop bills or statements.

b.h: What families often do with the mail

list: Keeping every bill and statement in one folder
Making a list of each company that writes, for closing accounts later
Opening anything from a bank, insurer or government agency promptly

b.tip: A few months of mail is often the most complete list of accounts a family will ever get. Many executors wait at least a full year before stopping forwarding, so annual bills and tax forms arrive too.

t: Notifying Social Security
pre: Often the funeral home does it. A few things are still up to the family.

b.p: The Social Security Administration needs to know about a death to stop payments and check for survivor benefits. In most cases, the funeral home reports the death to Social Security, using the information the family gives them.

If no funeral home is involved, or the family wants to make sure the death was reported, they can call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213, or visit a local office. The SSA doesn't accept death reports online. Having the person's Social Security number ready helps.

Social Security pays benefits a month behind. A person isn't due a payment for the month they die, so a payment that arrives the following month usually has to be returned. If it was a direct deposit, the bank is usually asked to return it.

list: A one-time death payment of $255, paid to a surviving spouse or child who meets certain requirements. It has to be applied for within 2 years.
Monthly survivor benefits, for a widow or widower, children, or sometimes dependent parents, depending on the person's work record

b.p: Survivor benefits aren't automatic in every case. Families usually need to apply by phone or at an office.

b.tip: Social Security shares death information with some other federal agencies, but not everyone. Medicare is usually updated automatically; banks, pensions and private insurers aren't.

t: Notifying an employer and claiming workplace benefits
pre: A job can leave behind more than a final paycheck.

b.p: If the person was working when they died, their employer usually has money and benefits to pay out. Some of these have deadlines, so families often contact HR within the first few weeks.

list: The final paycheck, and in some states, unused vacation pay. State laws vary.
Group life insurance, often one or two times salary, sometimes with extra coverage the person bought
Retirement accounts like a 401(k) or 403(b), which go to the named beneficiary
A pension, if there is one, which may pay a survivor benefit
Stock options, bonuses or commissions that were owed

b.p: If the family was covered through the person's job, coverage usually ends soon after the death. When a covered employee dies, the federal COBRA law usually lets their spouse and dependents keep the same coverage for up to 36 months, though they pay the full cost. COBRA generally applies to employers with 20 or more employees, and many states have similar rules for smaller ones.
Losing job-based coverage also allows the family to sign up for a marketplace plan at HealthCare.gov outside the usual enrollment period, usually within 60 days.

list: A certified copy of the death certificate
The beneficiary's details for each benefit
Sometimes proof of the executor's authority

b.tip: Former employers can matter too. An old pension or a 401(k) left at a past job still pays out. The US Department of Labor's free Retirement Savings Lost and Found database can help find plans from former employers.

current.label: COBRA for family after an employee's death
Employer size COBRA usually applies to
Marketplace sign-up window after losing coverage

t: Notifying the credit bureaus to prevent identity theft
pre: A name and Social Security number can still be misused after death.

b.p: Identity thieves sometimes use the details of people who have died, because no one is watching the accounts. Telling the three credit bureaus about a death helps stop new credit being opened in the person's name.

Equifax, Experian and TransUnion each accept death notices, usually by mail. The family member or executor typically sends a letter with a copy of the death certificate, proof of their role (such as letters testamentary), and the person's full name, date of birth, Social Security number and last address. The bureau then marks the file as deceased.
Social Security may eventually report the death, but it can take time and doesn't always reach every bureau. Many families contact all three directly.
The executor or a surviving spouse can usually request the person's credit report. It lists open credit cards and loans, which helps with closing accounts and spotting anything suspicious.

list: Leaving the person's age and date of birth out of a published obituary
Shredding mail with account numbers
Closing credit cards rather than leaving them open
Reporting any suspicious activity at IdentityTheft.gov

b.tip: Each bureau's mailing address and requirements change from time to time. Searching "[bureau name] report a deceased person" usually finds the current process.

t: Freezing vs. closing bank accounts
pre: Some accounts stop, some keep going, and some pass straight to someone else.

b.p: When a bank learns about a death, what happens next depends on how the account is set up. Many families are surprised to find a bank account frozen just when bills need paying.

table: How the account is set up
In one person's name only, no beneficiary
Frozen. Only the executor can access it, usually after probate or with a small-estate affidavit.
Joint account with right of survivorship
Passes to the other owner, who can usually keep using it
Paid to the beneficiary once they show a death certificate and ID

b.p: A frozen account can't be used for new withdrawals, checks or card payments. Automatic payments from it may stop. Deposits may still come in, but some, like Social Security payments for the month after the death, are usually pulled back.

Executors often open an estate bank account in the estate's name. Money from frozen accounts goes there, and the estate's bills are paid from it. Most banks require letters testamentary and a tax ID number for the estate.
Many states have a simpler process for smaller estates, often called a small-estate affidavit. The limits vary widely by state.

b.tip: Using a debit card or writing checks from someone's account after they die, even to pay their bills, can cause legal trouble for whoever does it. Many families wait until the executor has authority.

t: Cremation: what it costs and what the options are
pre: Simpler and usually cheaper than burial, with more choices than people expect.

b.p: Cremation is now chosen by more US families than burial, and cost is one of the most common reasons. It also leaves more room for choices about when and how to hold a service.

table: Transfer, the cremation itself, a basic container and the return of ashes. No viewing or service beforehand.
Direct cremation, plus a service later with or without the ashes present
Cremation with a viewing or funeral first
Embalming, a rental or purchased casket, a viewing or service, then cremation

b.p: According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the national median cost of a funeral with viewing and cremation was $6,280 in 2023. Direct cremation is usually far less, and prices vary a lot by region and provider.

list: Whether the quoted price includes the death certificate, the cremation permit and the medical examiner's fee, which some areas charge
Whether a casket is needed. It isn't. Under the federal Funeral Rule, a funeral home offering direct cremation has to make a simple alternative container available.
How long it takes. Many states require a waiting period, often 24 to 48 hours, before cremation can happen.
Whether the urn has to come from the provider. It doesn't. Any container can be used.

b.h: What people do with the ashes

list: Keeping them at home
Burying them in a cemetery plot or a niche in a columbarium
Scattering them somewhere meaningful. Rules for public land, parks and water vary, and scattering at sea is covered by federal rules.
Dividing them among family members

b.tip: There's no deadline for deciding what to do with the ashes. Many families wait months, or until a meaningful date.
